entries.name: Bubble Sort
entries.problem: Orders a short list of comparable values by repeatedly swapping out-of-order neighbors.
entries.intuition: Imagine shaking a list so adjacent items compare and the heavier ones slowly drift to the end each pass.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable elements.
entries.outputs: Same collection arranged in non-decreasing order.
steps: Compare the current element with the next element.
Swap if the pair is out of order.
Move one position forward and repeat until the pass ends.
Shrink the unsorted tail and loop until a pass produces no swaps.
entries.time_complexity: O(n²) average/worst, O(n) best when already sorted.
strengths: Simple to code and reason about.
Detects nearly-sorted input quickly if optimized to stop early.
weaknesses: Quadratic runtime makes it impractical for medium or large inputs.
Performs many redundant comparisons.
entries.explanation: Keep comparing neighbors so misplaced values crawl to the edges; repeat until no swaps happen.

entries.name: Insertion Sort
entries.problem: Maintains a growing sorted prefix by inserting each new value into its proper place.
entries.intuition: Like sorting playing cards: keep the hand sorted and slide each new card into position.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable items.
entries.outputs: Same collection sorted in ascending order.
steps: Treat the first element as sorted.
Shift larger elements in the sorted prefix one step to the right.
Insert the key into the freed slot.
Advance to the next element and repeat until the array is consumed.
entries.example: [4, 2, 5] → insert 2 before 4 ⇒ [2, 4, 5] → insert 5 (already in place).
entries.time_complexity: O(n²) average/worst, O(n) best on nearly-sorted data.
strengths: Excellent on tiny or almost sorted datasets.
weaknesses: Quadratic when many elements are out of order.
Heavy shifting work for long lists.
entries.explanation: Grow a sorted prefix and carefully insert each new element where it belongs.

entries.name: Selection Sort
entries.problem: Sorts by repeatedly selecting the smallest remaining element and placing it at the front.
entries.intuition: Scan the pile for the tiniest card, put it next in line, and continue with the leftovers.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable values.
steps: Set the current position i to 0.
Find the smallest element from i to end.
Swap that element with position i.
Increment i and repeat until the list is ordered.
entries.example: [7, 3, 5] → smallest is 3, swap with 7 ⇒ [3, 7, 5]; next smallest is 5, swap ⇒ [3, 5, 7].
strengths: Easy to reason about and implement.
weaknesses: Still quadratic in comparisons.
Not stable without extra work.
entries.explanation: Repeatedly locate the smallest unused value and stick it at the next slot of the sorted prefix.

entries.name: Heap Sort
entries.problem: Sorts by turning the input into a heap and repeatedly extracting the max (or min).
entries.intuition: Build a priority queue so the largest element can be removed and placed at the end one by one.
steps: Swap the root (largest value) with the last element.
Reduce the heap size by one and heapify the root.
Repeat extraction and heapify until one element remains.
entries.example: [4, 1, 3, 2] → build max-heap [4,2,3,1] → swap 4/1 ⇒ [1,2,3,4]; heapify remaining ⇒ [3,2,1,4] → continue until sorted.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) for all cases.
entries.space_complexity: O(1) extra space besides recursion-free heapify.
weaknesses: Not stable.
Constant factors higher than quick sort on average.
entries.explanation: Leverage the heap property so the largest item is always on top, remove it, and restore the heap repeatedly.

entries.name: Merge Sort
entries.problem: Efficiently sorts large lists by divide-and-conquer merging of sorted halves.
entries.intuition: Split the deck until each pile has one card, then merge piles back together in order.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable elements.
steps: Divide the array into two halves.
Merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.
Continue merging until a single sorted list remains.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) for all cases.
strengths: Great for linked lists and external sorting.
weaknesses: Requires extra memory for merging.
Recursive overhead on constrained environments.
entries.explanation: Keep splitting into halves until singles, then merge each pair while keeping them sorted.

entries.name: Quick Sort
entries.problem: Efficient in-place sort that partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts partitions.
entries.intuition: Pick a pivot, move smaller items left and larger right, then repeat on the two sides.
entries.outputs: Array sorted ascending or descending based on comparator.
steps: Partition the array so items < pivot go left, > pivot go right.
Recursively quick sort the left partition.
Recursively quick sort the right partition.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst if pivots are poor.
weaknesses: Worst-case quadratic when pivots are unbalanced.
Not stable by default.
entries.explanation: Divide around an intelligently chosen pivot so the partitions shrink quickly, leading to near-logarithmic depth.

entries.name: Bucket Sort
entries.problem: Sorts uniformly distributed real numbers by scattering them into buckets and sorting each bucket.
entries.intuition: Partition the [0,1) range into buckets so each holds a small local list that can be sorted quickly.
entries.inputs: List of real numbers typically normalized to [0, 1).
steps: Distribute each element into the appropriate bucket based on value.
Sort individual buckets (often using insertion sort).
entries.time_complexity: Average O(n) when distribution is uniform; worst O(n²) if items clump.
strengths: Buckets can be processed in parallel.
weaknesses: Performance degrades on skewed data.
Requires knowledge of value distribution.
entries.explanation: Exploit the distribution shape so each bucket is tiny, making local sorts trivial.

entries.name: Counting Sort
entries.problem: Sorts integers from a limited range by counting occurrences instead of comparing.
entries.intuition: Count how many times each value appears, then rebuild the list in order using counts as guides.
entries.inputs: List of integers within a known small range.
entries.outputs: Stable sorted list of the same integers.
steps: Determine the min and max values.
Allocate a counts array covering the range.
Optionally convert counts to prefix sums for stability.
Write elements back in order using the counts.
entries.time_complexity: O(n + k) where k is range size.
strengths: Linear time when k ≪ n log n.
Stable if prefix sums are used.
weaknesses: Requires known, limited range.
Extra memory proportional to range size.
entries.explanation: Use frequency counts rather than comparisons, making it lightning-fast on bounded integer domains.

entries.name: Radix Sort
entries.problem: Sorts integers or fixed-length strings by processing digits from least to most significant (or vice versa).
entries.intuition: Group numbers by each digit place using a stable sorter so positions eventually align globally.
steps: - Group elements by digit using a stable bucket (like counting sort).
- Concatenate buckets to reform the list.
Stop once the most significant digit is processed.
entries.example: [170, 45, 75, 90] ⇒ bucket by units, then tens, then hundreds ⇒ [45, 75, 90, 170].
entries.time_complexity: O(d · (n + k)) where d is digit count and k bucket size.
weaknesses: Needs stable sub-sorting and uniform key lengths.
Extra memory for buckets.
entries.explanation: Repeatedly bucket by digit so that by the final pass the entire key ordering emerges.

entries.name: Binary Search
entries.problem: Finds a target in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search interval.
entries.intuition: Like guessing a number: choose the midpoint, discard the half where the answer cannot live, repeat.
entries.outputs: Index of target or -1 if missing.
steps: Set low and high pointers to the bounds.
If array[mid] equals target, return mid.
If target < array[mid], move high to mid - 1.
Else move low to mid + 1 and repeat until low > high.
entries.example: Search 9 in [1,3,5,7,9,11]: mid=5→value=7 < 9, shift low ⇒ new mid=9 found at index 4.
strengths: Very fast on massive sorted arrays.
weaknesses: Requires sorted data with random access.
Insertion/deletion may break order.
entries.explanation: Keep cutting the remaining range in half so the number of candidates collapses exponentially.

entries.name: Interpolation Search
entries.problem: Searches uniformly distributed sorted data by estimating the likely position of the target.
entries.intuition: Instead of always probing the middle, interpolate where the target might land based on value range.
entries.inputs: Sorted list with roughly uniform distribution and the target.
steps: Estimate pos = low + (target - arr[low]) * (high - low) / (arr[high] - arr[low]).
If arr[pos] equals target, return pos.
If target < arr[pos], move high to pos - 1; else move low to pos + 1.
Repeat until low > high or value found.
entries.example: In [10,20,30,40,50], searching 40 calculates pos near index 3 immediately.
entries.time_complexity: O(log log n) average on uniform data, O(n) worst if distribution is skewed.
strengths: Fewer probes than binary search on uniform keys.
weaknesses: Performance collapses on clustered data.
Requires numeric keys with known range.
entries.explanation: Guess where the target should live based on proportional distance, probe there, and tighten the bounds.

entries.name: Jump Search
entries.problem: Balances linear and binary search by jumping ahead fixed blocks in a sorted array.
entries.intuition: Skip ahead in strides; once you overshoot, do a short linear scan backward.
steps: Jump ahead by step size until value ≥ target or end reached.
Perform linear search backward within the block where target could reside.
entries.example: [1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15], target 9, step=2: jump indices 0→2→4 (value 9) stop and confirm.
strengths: Fewer comparisons than linear search on sorted data.
weaknesses: Still slower than binary search.
Requires random access to jump.
entries.explanation: Hop through the array in fixed leaps, then crawl a short distance to find the exact slot.

entries.name: Linear Search
entries.problem: Finds the position of a target value by scanning elements sequentially.
entries.intuition: Check each item in order until the desired one appears or the list ends.
entries.outputs: Index of the target or -1 if absent.
steps: Otherwise advance to the next index.
Stop after the final element and return -1 if not found.
entries.example: Search 7 in [4, 7, 1]: compare 4 (no), compare 7 (yes) ⇒ index 1.
entries.time_complexity: O(n) average and worst; O(1) best if first element matches.
strengths: Simple to implement and reason about.
weaknesses: Slow on large datasets due to full scan.
Cannot skip work without extra structure.
entries.explanation: Walk through each entry until the goal appears; trivial but potentially time-consuming.

entries.name: AVL Tree
entries.problem: Maintains a self-balancing binary search tree where the heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most one.
entries.intuition: Like a see-saw that automatically adjusts itself: whenever one side gets too heavy, it rotates to balance out.
entries.inputs: Sequence of insert/delete/search operations on key-value pairs.
entries.outputs: Balanced binary search tree with O(log n) height guarantees.
steps: Insert or delete a node using standard BST rules.
Check the balance factor (height difference) of each ancestor.
Single rotation for outside cases (left-left or right-right).
Double rotation for inside cases (left-right or right-left).
Update heights and continue up the tree until balanced.
entries.example: Insert 3,2,1: After 3 and 2, insert 1 causes left-left imbalance. Rotate right around 3: [2(1,3)].
entries.time_complexity: O(log n) for all operations (insert, delete, search).
strengths: Guaranteed O(log n) height ensures predictable performance.
Strict balancing prevents worst-case O(n) behavior.
weaknesses: More complex than basic BST due to rotation overhead.
Requires storing balance factors or heights per node.
entries.explanation: A self-adjusting BST that keeps itself balanced by rotating nodes when one subtree becomes too tall.

entries.name: Binary Search Tree
entries.problem: Stores keys so that lookups, inserts, and deletes can exploit sorted order with O(log n) average time.
entries.intuition: Think of a game of twenty questions: each comparison decides whether to go left (smaller) or right (larger) until you reach the answer.
entries.inputs: Comparable keys with optional values; operations like insert, search, delete.
entries.outputs: Tree structure where in-order traversal yields sorted keys.
steps: Start at the root node and compare the target key.
If key < current node, recurse or iterate into the left child.
If key > current node, recurse or iterate into the right child.
If key equals the node, update or return the value.
During deletion, replace removed nodes with predecessor or successor to preserve ordering.
entries.example: Insert 8,3,10,1,6: 8 is root, 3 goes left, 10 right, 1 left of 3, 6 right of 3.
entries.time_complexity: Average O(log n); worst-case O(n) on skewed trees.
strengths: Maintains sorted order with simple pointer structure.
Supports inorder traversal to produce sorted output quickly.
weaknesses: Unbalanced input degrades operations to O(n).
Needs balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black) for guaranteed performance.
entries.explanation: A search tree where each node’s left subtree holds smaller keys and the right subtree holds larger ones, enabling logarithmic search when balanced.

entries.name: Binary Tree
entries.problem: Represents hierarchical relationships where each node may have up to two children.
entries.intuition: Picture a family tree where every person can have a left and right child pointer, letting you organize data hierarchically.
entries.inputs: Nodes containing data plus optional left/right child references.
entries.outputs: Tree structure supporting traversals such as preorder, inorder, and postorder.
steps: Create a root node (which may be empty).
Attach left/right children as required by the domain problem.
Traverse using preorder (node-left-right), inorder (left-node-right), or postorder (left-right-node).
Breadth-first traversal visits nodes level by level.
Perform application-specific work (search, aggregation) during traversals.
entries.example: Tree with root 1, left child 2, right child 3: inorder traversal yields [2,1,3].
entries.time_complexity: Traversals and searches touch each node once: O(n).
entries.space_complexity: O(n) for nodes plus O(h) recursion depth where h is tree height.
strengths: Flexible backbone for heaps, BSTs, and expression trees.
Natural fit for recursive definitions and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
weaknesses: By itself offers no ordering or balancing guarantees.
Pointer-heavy representation can hurt cache locality.
entries.explanation: A generic two-child-per-node structure that underpins many specialized tree variants and traversals.

entries.name: Avl Tree
entries.intuition: Avl Tree is a fundamental algorithm in computer science.
steps: Process input according to algorithm logic
entries.example: Example: Avl Tree applied to sample data.
weaknesses: May have limitations in certain scenarios
entries.explanation: Avl Tree solves computational problems efficiently.

entries.name: B-Tree
entries.problem: Efficiently stores and retrieves large datasets on disk by minimizing disk I/O through wide, shallow trees.
entries.intuition: Like a library filing system: instead of narrow tall shelves, use wide shallow ones so you can grab multiple books at once.
entries.inputs: Large dataset of key-value pairs, typically stored on disk.
entries.outputs: Multi-way search tree optimized for external storage access.
steps: Each node contains multiple keys (typically 100-1000) and child pointers.
Search: traverse from root, compare with node keys, follow appropriate child.
Insert: find leaf, add key; if node overflows, split and promote middle key.
Delete: remove key; if node underflows, merge with sibling or borrow key.
Maintain property: all leaves at same depth, nodes between t-1 and 2t-1 keys.
entries.example: B-tree of order 3: root [10,20] has children [5,7], [15,17], [25,27]. Insert 12: goes to middle child, no split needed.
entries.time_complexity: O(log n) with base of node capacity (typically 100-1000), making it effectively O(log n / log t).
entries.space_complexity: O(n) total storage, but nodes are large (disk pages).
strengths: Minimizes disk I/O by reading large nodes (pages) at once.
Widely used in databases and file systems for indexing.
weaknesses: More complex than binary trees for in-memory operations.
Requires careful tuning of node size for optimal performance.
entries.explanation: A multi-way tree that stores many keys per node to reduce disk reads, perfect for database indexing.

entries.name: Red-Black Tree
entries.problem: Maintains a balanced binary search tree with relaxed balancing rules compared to AVL trees.
entries.intuition: A BST with color coding: red and black nodes follow rules that keep the tree roughly balanced without strict height requirements.
entries.inputs: Sequence of insert/delete/search operations on key-value pairs.
entries.outputs: Balanced binary search tree with O(log n) worst-case height.
steps: Insert node as red (maintains black height property).
If parent is black, done; if red, check uncle color.
If uncle is red: recolor parent, uncle, and grandparent.
If uncle is black: rotate to fix red-red violation.
Root is always black; all paths have same black node count.
entries.example: Insert 5,3,7,1: After 1, red-red violation with 3. Uncle 7 is red, so recolor: 3 and 7 become black, 5 becomes red.
entries.time_complexity: O(log n) for all operations; slightly faster than AVL due to fewer rotations.
entries.space_complexity: O(n) with one color bit per node.
strengths: Fewer rotations than AVL trees, better for frequent updates.
Used in many standard library implementations (Java TreeMap, C++ map).
weaknesses: Less strictly balanced than AVL (height can be up to 2*log(n+1)).
More complex than basic BST.
entries.explanation: A self-balancing BST using red/black coloring rules that ensure no path is more than twice as long as any other.

entries.name: Trie
entries.problem: Efficiently stores and searches strings with shared prefixes, enabling fast prefix matching and autocomplete.
entries.intuition: Like a phone book organized by first letter, then second, then third: each level narrows down the search.
entries.inputs: Set of strings (words, keys) and query operations (insert, search, prefix match).
entries.outputs: Tree structure where each path from root to node represents a string prefix.
steps: Each node has children for each possible next character.
Insert: traverse/create path for each character, mark end node.
Search: follow path character by character, check if end marker exists.
Prefix search: traverse to prefix node, collect all descendants.
entries.example: Insert 'cat', 'car': root → 'c' → 'a' → 't' (end) and 'a' → 'r' (end). Search 'car': follow c-a-r, found.
entries.time_complexity: O(m) for search/insert where m is string length; O(n*m) to build from n strings.
entries.space_complexity: O(ALPHABET_SIZE * N * M) worst case, but can be compressed.
strengths: Fast prefix matching and autocomplete queries.
Efficient for dictionary lookups and spell checkers.
weaknesses: High memory usage for sparse tries.
Slower than hash tables for exact lookups.
entries.explanation: A tree where each path spells out a string, making prefix searches as fast as following the path.

entries.name: Binary Heap
entries.problem: Maintains a complete binary tree where parent nodes are always greater (max-heap) or smaller (min-heap) than children.
entries.intuition: Like a family tree where parents always outrank children: the top person is the most important, and you can quickly promote someone up the ranks.
entries.inputs: Sequence of insert/extract operations on priority values.
entries.outputs: Heap structure with O(1) access to max/min element.
steps: Store heap in array: parent at i, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
Insert: add to end, bubble up by swapping with parent if out of order.
Extract: remove root, move last element to root, bubble down by swapping with larger/smaller child.
Maintain heap property: parent >= children (max-heap) or parent <= children (min-heap).
entries.example: Max-heap [9,7,5,3,2]: Insert 8 → [9,7,5,3,2,8] → bubble up: [9,8,5,3,2,7] (8 swapped with 7's parent).
entries.time_complexity: O(log n) insert/extract, O(1) peek, O(n) build from array.
strengths: Efficient for priority queues and heap sort.
weaknesses: No efficient search or decrease-key without additional structures.
Not suitable for merging heaps efficiently.
entries.explanation: A complete binary tree stored in an array that keeps the highest (or lowest) priority item at the top with O(log n) updates.

entries.name: Fibonacci Heap
entries.problem: Provides extremely fast decrease-key and merge operations for advanced graph algorithms like Dijkstra's.
entries.intuition: A lazy heap: it defers organizing work until absolutely necessary, making most operations very fast on average.
entries.inputs: Sequence of insert, extract-min, decrease-key, and merge operations.
entries.outputs: Amortized O(1) insert and decrease-key, O(log n) extract-min.
steps: Maintain a collection of heap-ordered trees (forest).
Insert: add new single-node tree to forest, O(1).
Extract-min: remove min root, merge its children into forest, consolidate trees of same degree, O(log n).
Decrease-key: update node, cut from parent if violates heap property, mark parent, O(1) amortized.
entries.example: Forest with trees of degrees 0,1,2. Insert creates degree-0 tree. Extract-min consolidates: merge same-degree trees.
entries.time_complexity: O(1) amortized insert/decrease-key/merge, O(log n) amortized extract-min.
entries.space_complexity: O(n) with additional pointers for decrease-key operations.
strengths: Fastest known heap for decrease-key operations.
Enables O(m + n log n) Dijkstra's algorithm.
weaknesses: Complex implementation with many pointer manipulations.
Large constant factors make it slower than binary heap for small inputs.
entries.explanation: A sophisticated heap that delays consolidation work, achieving O(1) decrease-key for graph algorithms.

entries.name: Priority Queue
entries.problem: Manages elements where highest (or lowest) priority item is always accessible, regardless of insertion order.
entries.intuition: Like a hospital emergency room: the most urgent case gets treated first, even if others arrived earlier.
entries.inputs: Sequence of enqueue (insert) and dequeue (extract) operations with priority values.
entries.outputs: Always returns the highest priority element on dequeue.
steps: Choose underlying data structure (binary heap, Fibonacci heap, etc.).
Enqueue: insert element with its priority value.
Dequeue: extract and return element with highest/lowest priority.
Update priority: modify existing element's priority (if supported).
Maintain heap property to ensure O(log n) operations.
entries.example: Enqueue tasks: (A,5), (B,9), (C,3). Dequeue returns B (priority 9), then A (5), then C (3).
entries.time_complexity: O(log n) enqueue/dequeue with binary heap; O(1) amortized with Fibonacci heap.
strengths: Essential for scheduling, graph algorithms, and event simulation.
weaknesses: No efficient random access or search operations.
Requires total ordering of priorities.
entries.explanation: A data structure that always gives you the most important item first, perfect for scheduling and optimization.

entries.name: Hash Table with Chaining
entries.problem: Stores key-value pairs with O(1) average-case lookup by using hash function and collision resolution via linked lists.
entries.intuition: Like a library with numbered shelves: hash function tells you which shelf, chaining handles when multiple books share a shelf.
entries.inputs: Key-value pairs and operations: insert, get, delete.
entries.outputs: Fast O(1) average-case retrieval of values by key.
steps: Choose hash function h(k) that maps keys to bucket indices.
Insert: compute h(key), add (key,value) to linked list at that bucket.
Get: compute h(key), search linked list at bucket for matching key.
Delete: compute h(key), remove node from linked list at bucket.
Handle collisions: multiple keys hashing to same bucket share the list.
entries.example: Hash table size 5, keys 7,12,17. h(7)=2, h(12)=2 (collision), h(17)=2 (collision). Bucket 2: [7→12→17].
entries.time_complexity: O(1) average case, O(n) worst case if all keys hash to same bucket.
entries.space_complexity: O(n) for n key-value pairs plus overhead for buckets.
strengths: Simple collision resolution, easy to implement.
weaknesses: Worst-case O(n) if hash function is poor or keys are adversarial.
Requires good hash function and load factor management.
entries.explanation: A fast lookup structure that uses a hash function to map keys to buckets, with linked lists handling collisions.

entries.name: Hash Table
entries.problem: Provides constant-time average access to key-value pairs using hashing and collision resolution.
entries.intuition: Like placing labeled folders into numbered drawers: the hash function turns a key into a drawer index so you jump straight there.
entries.inputs: Key-value pairs with operations insert, lookup, delete.
entries.outputs: Table of buckets where each bucket stores entries that hash to the same index.
steps: Select hash function h(key) that maps keys to indices 0..m-1.
Insert: compute index, place entry in bucket (or follow collision policy).
Lookup: hash key, scan bucket/probe sequence for matching key.
Delete: hash key, remove entry while preserving collision structure.
Resize when load factor grows to keep operations near O(1).
entries.example: Table size 7, keys 'cat','dog','eel'. Hash to indices 2,5,2 respectively; bucket 2 stores ['cat','eel'].
entries.time_complexity: Average O(1) for insert/lookup/delete; worst-case O(n) if collisions degenerate.
entries.space_complexity: O(n) for entries plus bucket overhead.
strengths: Simple API for associative arrays and caches.
weaknesses: Needs high-quality hash functions and resizing strategy.
No inherent ordering of keys.
entries.explanation: Maps keys to array indices via a hash function so most operations touch a single bucket, yielding near-constant time.

entries.name: Open Addressing
entries.problem: Resolves hash table collisions by probing alternative slots instead of storing overflow lists.
entries.intuition: If a parking spot is taken, keep moving to the next slot according to a probe rule until you find an empty space.
entries.inputs: Fixed-size table and probe sequence (linear, quadratic, double hashing).
entries.outputs: Array where each slot holds at most one key-value pair plus optional tombstone markers.
steps: Hash key to initial index i0 = h(key).
If slot empty, place entry; otherwise compute next probe index via strategy.
Repeat probing until an empty slot or tombstone is found.
Lookup follows the same probe sequence until key or empty slot encountered.
Deletion marks slot as tombstone to preserve probe chains.
entries.example: Linear probing size 5: insert keys hashing to index 2. Occupied? Try 3, then 4, then wrap to 0.
entries.time_complexity: Average O(1) with low load factor; degrades toward O(n) as table fills.
entries.space_complexity: O(m) for table of m slots; no extra pointers.
strengths: Excellent cache locality because all data lives in the array.
No extra heap allocations compared to chaining.
weaknesses: Primary clustering can create long probe sequences.
Deletion logic complicated by tombstones and probe-chain maintenance.
entries.explanation: Keeps every key directly in the array, using probe sequences to find the next available slot whenever collisions occur.

entries.name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
entries.problem: Computes single-source shortest paths even when negative edge weights are present (assuming no negative cycles).
entries.intuition: Relax every edge repeatedly so distances shrink over successive passes; if they still shrink after |V|-1 rounds, a negative cycle exists.
entries.inputs: Directed weighted graph G(V,E) and source vertex s.
entries.outputs: Shortest path distances (and optionally predecessors) from s or detection of negative cycles.
steps: Initialize distance[s]=0 and all other distances to +∞.
Repeat |V|-1 times: for each edge (u,v,w), relax by setting dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w).
Track predecessors when an edge improves a distance.
Perform one more pass; if any edge can still relax, report a negative cycle.
entries.space_complexity: O(|V|) for distance and predecessor arrays.
weaknesses: Slower than Dijkstra on graphs without negative edges.
Detecting negative cycles requires an additional pass.
entries.explanation: Iteratively relaxes all edges to propagate better distances, making it robust for graphs with negative weights.

entries.name: Breadth-First Search
entries.problem: Traverses graphs level by level to find the shortest path in unweighted graphs and to explore reachable vertices.
entries.intuition: Expand the frontier like ripples in a pond: visit all vertices one edge away before moving farther out.
entries.inputs: Graph G(V,E) and optional start vertex.
entries.outputs: Visit order, distance in edges, and predecessor tree for shortest paths.
steps: Mark the start vertex as discovered, set distance 0, and enqueue it.
While the queue is not empty, dequeue vertex u.
For each neighbor v of u: if undiscovered, mark it, set parent[v]=u, dist[v]=dist[u]+1, enqueue v.
Continue until queue empty to explore connected component.
Use predecessor pointers to reconstruct shortest paths.
entries.example: Graph 0-1-2-3 with extra edge 0-2. BFS from 0 visits 0,1,2,3; dist[3]=2 via 0→2→3.
entries.space_complexity: O(|V|) for queue, visited, and parent arrays.
strengths: Guarantees shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Useful for level-order traversal, bipartite checking, and finding connected components.
weaknesses: Requires memory proportional to the frontier size.
Does not handle weights without modification.
entries.explanation: Uses a queue to expand vertices in increasing distance from the source, ensuring level-order exploration.

entries.name: Depth-First Search
entries.problem: Explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.
entries.intuition: Like navigating a maze by always taking the next unexplored corridor until you hit a dead end, then backing up.
entries.inputs: Graph representation plus optional start vertex.
entries.outputs: Discovery/finish times, parent tree, and traversal order.
steps: Start at chosen vertex, mark it visited, record discovery time.
Recursively visit each unvisited neighbor (or use an explicit stack).
After exploring neighbors, record finish time and backtrack.
Repeat for any unvisited vertex to cover disconnected components.
Leverage recorded times for cycle detection, topological sort, and strongly connected components.
entries.example: DFS on graph 0-1-2-3 explores path 0→1→2→3, then backtracks to explore remaining edges.
entries.space_complexity: O(|V|) recursion stack in worst case.
strengths: Foundation for algorithms like topological sort and SCCs.
Memory-light compared to BFS on dense layers.
weaknesses: Paths found are not guaranteed shortest.
Deep recursion can overflow the stack on large graphs.
entries.explanation: Explores one branch completely before moving to the next, making it ideal for exhaustive search and backtracking problems.

entries.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
entries.problem: Computes shortest paths from a single source in graphs with non-negative edge weights.
entries.intuition: Grow a settled set of nodes: always expand the vertex with the smallest tentative distance because no shorter route to it can exist.
entries.inputs: Graph with non-negative edge weights and source vertex.
entries.outputs: Shortest path distances and predecessors for each reachable vertex.
steps: Initialize distance[source]=0, others=∞; push source into priority queue.
Extract vertex u with smallest distance.
For each edge (u,v,w), relax: if dist[u]+w < dist[v], update and push v.
Mark u as settled so it will not be processed again.
Continue until queue empty; reconstruct paths from predecessor array.
entries.example: Edges A→B(2), A→C(5), B→C(1). Algorithm finds dist[C]=3 via A→B→C.
entries.space_complexity: O(|V|) for distance array and priority queue entries.
strengths: Fast on sparse graphs with non-negative weights.
Widely used in routing, navigation, and network optimization.
weaknesses: Fails with negative edge weights.
Priority queue operations dominate costs on dense graphs.
entries.explanation: Repeatedly selects the closest unsettled vertex and relaxes its edges, guaranteeing optimal distances when weights are non-negative.

entries.name: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
entries.problem: Computes all-pairs shortest paths on weighted graphs (positive or negative edges, excluding negative cycles).
entries.intuition: Dynamic programming over intermediate vertices: allow paths to use the first k vertices and iteratively increase k.
entries.inputs: Weighted adjacency matrix for graph with n vertices.
entries.outputs: n×n matrix of shortest path distances (and optionally predecessor matrix).
steps: Initialize dist[i][j] with edge weights, set dist[i][i]=0.
For k from 1 to n: for each pair (i,j), set dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
Optionally maintain next[i][j] to reconstruct paths.
After loops, dist contains shortest distances using any intermediate vertex.
Detect negative cycles if any dist[i][i] < 0.
entries.example: For 3-vertex graph, algorithm considers whether going through vertex 2 improves distance from 1 to 3 and updates matrix accordingly.
strengths: Handles negative weights and finds all-pairs distances in one pass.
weaknesses: Cubic runtime becomes expensive for large graphs.
Requires dense matrix storage even for sparse graphs.
entries.explanation: Systematically checks whether including each vertex k shortens the path between i and j, yielding all-pairs solutions.

entries.name: 0/1 Knapsack
entries.problem: Selects items with weights and values to maximize value without exceeding capacity, using each item at most once.
entries.intuition: Build solutions bottom-up: for each item, choose to take it or leave it based on remaining capacity and value gain.
entries.inputs: List of item weights and values plus knapsack capacity W.
entries.outputs: Maximum achievable value and optionally the chosen item set.
steps: Create DP table dp[i][w] = best value using first i items and capacity w.
For each item i and capacity w: if weight[i] > w, copy dp[i-1][w]; otherwise take max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w-weight[i]]).
Fill table row by row to capacity W.
Trace back from dp[n][W] to recover chosen items.
entries.example: Items {(2,3),(3,4),(4,5)}, capacity 5. Optimal takes items 1 and 2 for value 7.
entries.time_complexity: O(nW) where n items and capacity W.
entries.space_complexity: O(nW) table or O(W) with rolling array optimization.
strengths: Deterministic optimal solution when W is moderate.
Classic DP illustrating trade-offs in subset selection problems.
weaknesses: Pseudo-polynomial: runtime grows with numeric capacity.
Not suitable when fractional choices are allowed.
entries.explanation: Dynamic programming weighs the value of including each item versus skipping it, constrained by the remaining capacity.

entries.name: Dependency Inversion Principle
entries.problem: High-level modules should not depend on low-level details; both should rely on abstractions.
entries.intuition: Make policies depend on interfaces, not concrete wiring—like plugging different chargers into the same standard outlet.
entries.inputs: Tightly coupled modules where business logic instantiates infrastructure details.
entries.outputs: Abstractions (interfaces, ports) with concrete implementations supplied via inversion of control.
steps: Identify high-level policies that currently create or depend on concrete classes.
Define abstractions capturing the required behavior.
Make high-level code depend on the abstractions instead of concretes.
Provide implementations via constructors, factories, or DI containers.
Write integration tests that swap implementations to ensure decoupling.
entries.example: OrderService new EmailNotifier() → instead depend on Notifier interface and inject EmailNotifier or SmsNotifier.
entries.time_complexity: Adds indirection proportional to number of dependencies.
entries.space_complexity: Requires extra interfaces and binding configuration.
weaknesses: More abstractions can complicate debugging.
Needs tooling (DI containers) to stay manageable at scale.
entries.explanation: Depend on abstractions so high-level logic stays stable while low-level details swap freely.

entries.name: Interface Segregation Principle
entries.problem: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.
entries.intuition: Give each client a tailored remote control; bloated interfaces force consumers to worry about buttons they never press.
entries.inputs: Large interfaces implemented by many classes with empty or throwing methods.
entries.outputs: Smaller, client-specific interfaces implemented by relevant classes.
steps: List interface methods and map them to actual client usage.
Identify clusters of methods used together by specific clients.
Split the interface into cohesive sub-interfaces.
Update classes to implement only the interfaces they need.
Refactor clients to depend on the refined contracts.
entries.example: IMultiFunctionDevice exposes print/scan/fax; a scanner-only device should not implement fax, so split into IPrinter, IScanner, IFax.
entries.time_complexity: Refactor effort grows with number of clients.
strengths: Reduces stub methods and unused dependencies.
weaknesses: Too many interfaces can overwhelm newcomers.
Requires coordination when clients share overlapping needs.
entries.explanation: Favor many small interfaces over one large one so consumers only depend on what they actually use.

entries.name: Liskov Substitution Principle
entries.problem: Derived classes must behave like their base class so clients can substitute them without surprises.
entries.intuition: If a square is a rectangle, any rectangle-using code should still work when given a square; inheritance should not break contracts.
entries.inputs: Class hierarchies where overrides narrow behavior or violate expectations.
entries.outputs: Subclasses that preserve base invariants, preconditions, and postconditions.
steps: Document the base class contract (inputs, outputs, side effects).
Ensure subclasses do not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions.
Avoid throwing new exceptions or changing returned types unexpectedly.
Prefer composition when behavior diverges significantly.
Add substitution tests to validate behavior parity.
entries.example: Bird base class fly() → Penguin subclass overrides to throw; violates LSP, so extract FlightlessBird behavior instead.
entries.time_complexity: Focused on design correctness rather than runtime.
entries.space_complexity: May require extra wrapper classes for composition.
weaknesses: Hard to enforce without strong contracts/tests.
Legacy hierarchies may need large refactors.
entries.explanation: Subclasses should honor the promises of their parents so client code can substitute them freely.

entries.name: Open/Closed Principle
entries.problem: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification.
entries.intuition: Once stable, classes become plug-in sockets: add new behavior via extension points instead of editing core logic.
entries.inputs: Existing class that needs new behavior variations.
entries.outputs: Abstractions that allow new features through inheritance, composition, or configuration.
steps: Identify areas where features keep forcing edits to the same class.
Extract abstractions (interfaces, base classes, strategy objects).
Move variable behavior behind the abstraction boundary.
Register new implementations without touching existing code.
Cover extension points with tests to guard regressions.
entries.example: ShippingCalculator switches via if/else per region → introduce ShippingStrategy interface and register new strategies.
entries.time_complexity: Depends on the breadth of extension points.
entries.space_complexity: Additional classes or configuration objects to host extensions.
strengths: Limits regression risk when adding features.
weaknesses: Requires upfront abstraction design.
Over-abstraction can make code harder to follow.
entries.explanation: Design modules so you add new behavior by plugging in new classes, not by editing the old ones.

entries.name: Single Responsibility Principle
entries.problem: Ensures each class or module has exactly one reason to change.
entries.intuition: Treat classes like specialists: one job, done well, so changes in one concern don’t ripple through unrelated code.
entries.inputs: Object-oriented modules with multiple responsibilities entangled.
entries.outputs: Refactored components where each focuses on a single responsibility.
steps: Identify all reasons why the class might change (UI tweaks, business rules, persistence, etc.).
Group behaviors by responsibility and highlight unrelated clusters.
Extract new classes/functions for secondary responsibilities.
Inject dependencies so each class collaborates instead of owning all logic.
Add tests per responsibility to prove isolation.
entries.example: A Report class both formats PDFs and queries the database → split into ReportGenerator + ReportRepository.
entries.time_complexity: Refactoring effort proportional to responsibilities discovered.
strengths: Reduces blast radius when business rules evolve.
weaknesses: May introduce more classes/interfaces to navigate.
Requires discipline to maintain separation over time.
entries.explanation: Keep each module focused on one reason to change so maintenance stays local and predictable.

entries.name: Adapter Pattern
entries.problem: Allows incompatible interfaces to collaborate without modifying existing code.
entries.intuition: Like a power plug converter: adapt one shape to another so both sides work together.
entries.inputs: Client expecting interface A and an existing service implementing interface B.
entries.outputs: Adapter class translating client calls to the adaptee’s API.
steps: Identify the target interface the client expects.
Wrap the existing class (adaptee) inside an adapter implementing the target interface.
Translate each operation: convert parameters, call adaptee, convert results.
Inject or instantiate the adapter where the client previously used the adaptee.
Write tests ensuring the adapter faithfully forwards behavior.
entries.example: Legacy XmlLogger used by new JsonLogger clients; Adapter implements JsonLogger interface but delegates to XmlLogger.
entries.space_complexity: O(1) extra state per adapter instance.
strengths: Enables reuse of existing classes without altering them.
weaknesses: Adds another indirection layer to maintain.
Complex mappings can become brittle.
entries.explanation: Introduce a thin wrapper that exposes the interface you need while delegating real work to an incompatible class.

entries.name: Bridge Pattern
entries.problem: Decouples abstractions from their implementations so both can vary independently.
entries.intuition: Think of a remote control talking to different TVs: the remote is the abstraction, the TV electronics are implementations.
entries.inputs: Hierarchy where multiple dimensions of variation (e.g., shape vs. rendering API) would otherwise explode subclasses.
entries.outputs: Two orthogonal class hierarchies linked via composition.
steps: Split the abstraction (high-level operations) from the implementation (platform-specific work).
Define an implementation interface with primitive operations.
Have the abstraction hold a reference to the implementation and delegate calls.
Subclass both sides independently as variation requires.
Provide wiring (factories/DI) to pair abstraction with concrete implementation.
entries.example: Shape abstraction (Circle, Square) delegates draw() to Renderer implementation (VectorRenderer, RasterRenderer).
entries.time_complexity: Same as underlying implementation plus indirection.
entries.space_complexity: One reference from abstraction to implementation.
strengths: Prevents class explosion when combining variation axes.
weaknesses: More moving parts compared to simple inheritance.
Requires careful naming to keep roles clear.
entries.explanation: Compose abstractions with implementations so each can evolve on its own timeline without recompiling the other.

entries.name: Composite Pattern
entries.problem: Treats individual objects and compositions uniformly (tree structures).
entries.intuition: File systems treat files and directories with the same interface; composites hold children, leaves perform real work.
entries.inputs: Recursive structures needing hierarchical operations (rendering UI trees, calculating totals).
entries.outputs: Component interface with Leaf and Composite implementations.
steps: Define a common Component interface with operations clients need.
Implement Composite storing child components; delegate operations to children.
Ensure clients only depend on the Component interface.
entries.example: Graphic objects: Line, Circle (leaves) and Group (composite) so drawing occurs recursively.
entries.time_complexity: Operations typically traverse entire subtree: O(n) where n is number of nodes touched.
entries.space_complexity: O(n) to store tree plus recursion stack.
strengths: Simplifies client code—treat everything as Component.
weaknesses: Hard to restrict which composites may contain which components.
Can complicate operations needing parent references.
entries.explanation: Build tree structures where clients operate on components without caring if they’re leaves or composites.

entries.name: Decorator Pattern
entries.problem: Adds responsibilities to objects dynamically without subclass explosion.
entries.intuition: Like wrapping a gift multiple times: each wrapper adds behavior while still exposing the same interface.
entries.inputs: Base component with optional features (logging, caching, compression).
entries.outputs: Decorator classes implementing the same interface and holding a reference to the wrapped component.
steps: Define a Component interface implemented by the base class.
Create Decorator base class implementing Component and storing a Component reference.
Implement concrete decorators that augment behavior before/after delegating.
Wrap components with decorators at runtime to compose features.
Ensure removal/reordering of decorators remains simple.
entries.example: DataSource decorated with CompressionDecorator then EncryptionDecorator before writing to disk.
entries.time_complexity: Adds linear overhead proportional to number of decorators.
entries.space_complexity: O(k) extra objects for k decorators.
strengths: Flexible combination of features at runtime.
weaknesses: Debugging stack of decorators can be tricky.
Many small objects increase complexity.
entries.explanation: Wrap an object with other objects conforming to the same interface to add responsibilities dynamically.

entries.name: Facade Pattern
entries.problem: Provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
entries.intuition: Think customer service hotline: one number routes requests to myriad internal departments.
entries.inputs: Subsystem with many classes and configuration steps overwhelming clients.
entries.outputs: Facade class exposing coarse-grained operations that orchestrate underlying components.
steps: Map common client workflows that touch multiple subsystem classes.
Create a Facade exposing methods for each workflow.
Inside facade methods, coordinate subsystem objects in the right sequence.
Keep subsystem classes accessible for advanced clients when needed.
entries.example: VideoConverter facade hides codecs, bitrates, and file IO from client code.
entries.time_complexity: Same as orchestrated workflow; facade adds minimal overhead.
entries.space_complexity: Facade may cache subsystem instances for reuse.
strengths: Reduces learning curve for complicated APIs.
weaknesses: Facade can become a god-object if it grows unchecked.
Still requires subsystem access for edge cases.
entries.explanation: Offer a single entry point that bundles complex operations so clients interact with a friendly API.

entries.name: Proxy Pattern
entries.problem: Provides a surrogate object controlling access to a real subject (lazy loading, security, remote access).
entries.intuition: Like a personal assistant screening calls before they reach the executive.
entries.inputs: Original service object that needs access control, caching, or remote indirection.
entries.outputs: Proxy implementing the same interface and delegating to the real subject with extra logic.
steps: Define subject interface shared by both real object and proxy.
Proxy holds reference to real subject, instantiating it lazily if necessary.
Override operations to add pre/post behavior (checks, caching, logging).
Ensure client interacts only with the proxy interface.
Handle cleanup (connection closing, resource disposal) inside proxy.
entries.example: Virtual proxy delaying image loading until it must be displayed.
entries.time_complexity: Varies with added behavior (e.g., caching may improve average time).
entries.space_complexity: Proxy holds pointer to real subject plus any cache state.
strengths: Supports remote proxies for distributed systems.
weaknesses: Another abstraction layer to test and maintain.
Improper proxies can hide performance issues.
entries.explanation: Insert a stand-in object that looks like the real one but adds access control, caching, or remote communication.

entries.name: SQL Joins
entries.problem: Combine rows from related tables based on matching keys.
entries.intuition: Treat tables like sets and match rows where keys agree or complement each other.
entries.inputs: Two or more tables plus join condition.
entries.outputs: Composite rows containing columns from each source table.
steps: Choose join type (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS).
Relational engine decides join algorithm (nested loop, hash, merge).
entries.example: SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;
entries.time_complexity: Depends on join algorithm; hash join ~O(n + m), nested loop ~O(n·m) without indexes.
entries.space_complexity: May require hash tables or sort buffers.
strengths: Expressive way to relate normalized tables.
weaknesses: Expensive if keys lack indexes.
Incorrect join types can duplicate or drop rows.
entries.explanation: Map matching keys across tables so related data can be viewed as a single combined set.

entries.name: SQL Queries
entries.problem: Retrieve, filter, and manipulate relational data using declarative statements.
entries.intuition: Describe the desired result set while the optimizer chooses an execution plan.
entries.outputs: Result set, affected row count, or updated storage state.
steps: Generate a logical plan (joins, filters, projections).
Optimize into a physical plan using indexes and statistics.
Execute the plan and stream results back to the client.
entries.example: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country='Canada'; returns matching customer names.
entries.time_complexity: Varies; indexed lookups approach O(log n), full scans O(n).
entries.space_complexity: Driven by execution plan (temporary joins, sorting buffers).
strengths: Mature optimizers leverage indexes and caches.
weaknesses: Poorly written queries can degrade to full scans.
Requires understanding of indexes and statistics for tuning.
entries.explanation: State what data you want, let the relational engine decide how to fetch it efficiently.

entries.name: SQL Transactions
entries.problem: Bundle multiple statements into an atomic, consistent, isolated, durable unit of work.
entries.intuition: Either all operations succeed together or none do, safeguarding integrity even under failures.
entries.outputs: Committed data changes or a rollback to the previous state.
steps: BEGIN (implicit or explicit) starts a transaction context.
Execute one or more SQL statements.
If all succeed, issue COMMIT to persist changes.
On error or manual cancel, issue ROLLBACK to undo.
DBMS enforces ACID properties via logging and locking.
entries.example: Transfer funds: debit one account, credit another, COMMIT only if both succeed; else ROLLBACK.
entries.time_complexity: Depends on enclosed statements; logging adds small overhead.
entries.space_complexity: Requires log space for redo/undo records.
strengths: Protects data integrity under concurrency and crashes.
weaknesses: Excessive transaction scope can cause contention.
Long transactions hold locks, reducing throughput.
entries.explanation: Group related statements so they behave as a single all-or-nothing change, ensuring ACID guarantees.
